report:
Conclusion: Supported—with caveats. In children/adolescents with Dravet syndrome whose seizures remain uncontrolled, adjunctive pharmaceutical-grade cannabidiol (Epidiolex) reduces convulsive seizure frequency versus placebo, but it is not a cure and has clinically important adverse effects/interactions.

The pivotal double-blind RCT (n=120; ages ~2–18; CBD 20 mg/kg/day) found median convulsive-seizure frequency fell 38.9% with CBD vs 13.3% with placebo; more CBD patients had somnolence, decreased appetite, diarrhea, and aminotransferase elevations (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28813226/). A dose-ranging RCT (n=199) reported convulsive-seizure reductions of 48.7% (10 mg/kg/day) and 45.7% (20 mg/kg/day) vs 26.9% placebo, with similar efficacy and dose-related tolerability concerns (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7052786/). FDA labeling reflects this evidence and lists Dravet-syndrome seizure treatment as an indication, with warnings for hepatocellular injury and somnolence (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2018/210365lbl.pdf). A DS-focused systematic review/meta-analysis likewise concluded adjunctive CBD gives greater convulsive-seizure reduction than placebo but higher adverse-event rates (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32040850/).

Bottom line: true for regulated, purified CBD as add-on therapy under specialist supervision; do not extrapolate to unregulated CBD products, and monitor liver enzymes plus clobazam/valproate interactions.
